items.title: The Lost-and-Found Runway
items.text:
By February, the lost-and-found box outside our school
gym had turned into a mountain. It held jackets and
sweatshirts, a lunchbox nobody dared to open, one purple
rain boot, and enough mittens to fill a laundry basket.
Every Monday, our principal reminded everyone over the
loudspeaker to check the box. Every Monday, the mountain
grew a little taller.

Then our art teacher, Mr. Ferreira, had an idea. "Nobody
looks at a pile," he told our class. "But everybody
watches a show." He asked the principal if the fifth
grade could put on a fashion show at the Friday
assembly, with every outfit borrowed from the
lost-and-found.

Twelve of us volunteered to be models. On Thursday we
sorted the pile into outfits, which was harder than it
sounds. A striped scarf went with a green raincoat that
was much too big for any of us. The rain boot had no
partner, so Ruben wore it with one of his own sneakers.

On Friday, the gym lights dimmed and music thumped from
the speakers. A row of blue tumbling mats made a runway
down the middle of the floor. One by one, we strutted to
the end, turned, and posed while Mr. Ferreira described
each outfit like a television host. "Here we have a cozy
gray hoodie," he announced, "with half a granola bar
still in the pocket."

The first shout came from the third row: "That's mine!"
A second grader raced down to collect her hoodie, and
the whole gym cheered as if she had won a prize. After
that, hands shot up all over the room. A kindergartner
claimed a jacket that hung down to his knees; it
belonged to his big brother, who had been searching for
it since December.

By the end of the assembly, forty-one items had been
claimed. The rest were washed, folded, and given to a
clothing drive downtown. Only the purple rain boot was
left, and it now stands on the windowsill of the front
office, holding a bunch of paper flowers.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE; no real person, place or event is named.

items.title: Fur, Rocks, and Kelp
items.text:
A sea otter usually eats while floating on its back at
the surface of the ocean, using its own chest as a
table. When it naps, it often wraps itself in a long
strand of kelp so that it will not drift away. A group
of otters resting together is called a raft.

Unlike seals, sea otters have no thick layer of blubber
to keep them warm. Instead, they rely on the densest fur
of any animal. A single square inch of an otter's skin
can hold as many as a million hairs. The fur traps tiny
bubbles of air, which keep the cold water away from the
otter's skin. To keep its coat waterproof, an otter
spends hours every day cleaning and fluffing it.

Staying warm also uses an enormous amount of energy. To
keep up, a sea otter must eat about a quarter of its own
weight in food every day. It dives to the bottom for
crabs, clams, mussels, and sea urchins, and it tucks
what it catches into a loose pocket of skin under its
front leg. Back at the surface, it may crack open a hard
shell by pounding it against a rock, which some otters
even carry in that same pocket.

Those spiny sea urchins are more important than they
look. Urchins feed on kelp, a giant seaweed that can
grow 100 feet tall and forms thick forests under the
water. Thousands of tiny animals live among the kelp.
Where there are plenty of otters, they keep the urchins
in check. Where the otters disappear, the urchins can
multiply and chew through a kelp forest until the sea
floor is nearly bare. Scientists call such a place an
urchin barren.

For more than a hundred years, hunters killed sea otters
for their thick, soft fur. By 1900, only one or two
thousand were left in the whole world. In 1911, a treaty
between nations finally protected them, and during the
twentieth century their numbers recovered.
items.source: Facts verified against the Monterey Bay Aquarium pages 'Sea otter' (montereybayaquarium.org/animals-the-ocean/animals-a-to-z/sea-otter) and 'Giant kelp' (montereybayaquarium.org/animals-the-ocean/animals-a-to-z/giant-kelp); the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, 'Northern Sea Otter' (adfg.alaska.gov/index.cfm?adfg=seaotter.main); the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 'Southern Sea Otter' (fws.gov/species/southern-sea-otter-enhydra-lutris-nereis); the National Park Service, Kenai Fjords National Park, 'Sea Otter' (nps.gov/kefj/learn/nature/sea-otter.htm); and the Seattle Aquarium, 'The densest fur of any animal on earth' (seattleaquarium.org/stories/the-densest-fur-of-any-animal-on-earth-all-about-sea-otters). items.title: Something Out There
items.text:
Hattie and her cousin Quinn had begged all week to sleep
in the backyard, and on Friday evening Aunt Lou finally
dragged the old tent out of the garage. They set it up
beside the fence, lined up their sneakers just inside
the entrance, and told ghost stories until the beam of
their flashlight began to fade.

Then the noise began. It was a high, sharp chirp,
repeated over and over, as regular as a ticking clock.
Hattie sat up suddenly in her sleeping bag. "Do you hear
that?" she whispered.

Quinn was already listening. "It's probably a bird," he
said, but he did not sound certain. Birds did not
usually sing in the middle of the night. Stranger still,
the sound seemed to come from everywhere at once: from
the fence, from the grass, from the dark row of tomato
plants beside the porch.

They decided to investigate. Quinn shook the flashlight
until it produced a weak yellow glow, and the two of
them crept out of the tent in their socks. The grass was
icy and soaking wet. Every time they tiptoed toward the
fence, the chirping seemed to slip around behind them,
back toward the tent. They searched underneath the porch
steps and inside an empty flowerpot. Hattie even lifted
the lid of the sandbox, half expecting some creature to
leap out at her.

After twenty minutes they gave up and crawled back
inside, shivering. The moment Quinn zipped the door
shut, the chirping grew louder than ever. Hattie pointed
the dim flashlight at the row of sneakers. Very slowly,
Quinn lifted his left one. Sitting inside the toe was a
small brown cricket, its back legs folded and ready to
spring.

Quinn carried the sneaker outside and tipped it gently
over the grass. For a while the yard was completely
silent. Then, from somewhere near the fence, the
chirping started again, softer now and farther away, and
the two cousins were asleep before it stopped.

items.title: Twelve Dots, Then Six
items.text:
Louis Braille was born in 1809 in Coupvray, a village
near Paris, France. His father was a harness maker who
made leather gear for horses. One day, when Louis was
three, he was playing in the workshop with one of his
father's sharp tools, and he injured his eye. An
infection set in and spread to his other eye, and by the
age of five he was completely blind. Even so, he went on
to attend the village school for three years.

When Louis was ten, he won a scholarship to the Royal
Institute for Blind Youth, a school in Paris. The school
owned only a handful of books, printed in large raised
letters that students read by running their fingers over
them. Telling the curved letters apart was slow work.

In 1821, when Louis was twelve, an army captain named
Charles Barbier visited the school. Barbier had invented
a code called night writing, which allowed soldiers to
pass messages in the dark without speaking. Instead of
letters, it used raised dots, and Louis recognized that
dots could be the answer for blind readers. Yet
Barbier's code had problems. Its signs stood for sounds
rather than letters, and a single sign could need as
many as twelve dots, a shape too tall to feel all at
once.

Louis spent the next three years improving the code. He
reduced the number of dots to six, arranged in two
columns of three, and he made each pattern stand for a
letter. By 1824, when he was fifteen, his system was
finished. Six dots can be arranged in sixty-four
different ways, enough for letters, numbers, punctuation
marks, and even musical notes.

At seventeen, Louis became a teacher at the school, and
he also played the organ in churches around Paris. In
1829 he published a book that explained his system. He
died of tuberculosis in 1852, when he was forty-three
years old. Two years after his death, France officially
adopted his code of raised dots.
items.source: Facts verified against the Library of Congress, National Library Service, 'Braille 200' (loc.gov/nls/braille); the WIPO Magazine (World Intellectual Property Organization), 'Bicentenary of Louis Braille – The world at our fingertips' (wipo.int/en/web/wipo-magazine); the Musée Louis Braille, Coupvray, 'Biography' (museelouisbraille.com/en/biographie); the University of Houston, 'The Engines of Our Ingenuity', episode 2731 (engines.egr.uh.edu/episode/2731); and the American Foundation for the Blind chronology on the education of blind children (afb.org/about-afb/history/online-library/unseen-minority/historical-chronologies/history-education-visually). items.title: A Wave Carved in Wood
items.text:
One of the most famous pictures in the world is only
about ten inches tall and fifteen inches wide. It shows
a giant wave curling over a few sleek boats. The rowers
huddle low and cling to their oars. Far in the distance,
beneath the curl of the wave, sits Mount Fuji, looking
tiny.

The picture is known as The Great Wave. The Japanese
artist Katsushika Hokusai designed it for a series of
views of Mount Fuji. He began the series in 1830, when
he was seventy years old, and it helped make landscape
prints popular, as they still are today. Each picture
shows the mountain from a different direction, near or
far, in a different season or kind of weather. The boats
in The Great Wave were swift boats that carried fresh
fish to the markets of Edo, the city now called Tokyo.

Hokusai did not print the picture himself. Like other
artists of his time, he made only the design, a drawing
in lines with notes about the colors. A carver pasted
the drawing face down on a block of cherry wood and then
carved away everything except the lines. That first
block printed the outline of the picture. Next, the
carver cut a separate block for each color. He also cut
small marks at the edges so that the printer could line
up every color exactly.

The printer brushed color onto one block and laid a
sheet of paper on top. Then he rubbed the back of the
paper with a pad called a baren. He did the same with
the next block, and the next. For the sea and the sky,
Hokusai chose Berlin blue. This deep blue coloring had
only recently become cheap enough for printers to use.

Because the blocks could be inked again and again, the
same picture could be printed many times. The Art
Institute of Chicago owns three impressions of The Great
Wave. The National Gallery of Victoria, in Melbourne,
Australia, owns another.
items.source: Facts verified against the Art Institute of Chicago, 'Under the Wave off Kanagawa (Kanagawa oki nami ura), also known as The Great Wave' (artic.edu/artworks/24645 and 77333); the National Gallery of Victoria, Melbourne, 'The great wave off Kanagawa' (ngv.vic.gov.au/explore/collection/work/22076); the U.S. Geological Survey image page 'Hokusai, Under the Wave off Kanagawa' (usgs.gov/media/images/hokusai-under-wave-kanagawa); Japan House Los Angeles, 'The Process of Woodblock Printing' (japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/process-of-woodblock-printing); the Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford, Jameel Centre, on Japanese print production (jameelcentre.ashmolean.org/collection/7/10225/10238); and the Beaty Biodiversity Museum, University of British Columbia, 'Mokuhanga' (explore.beatymuseum.ubc.ca/peatland/process/mokuhanga) for the registration marks and the baren.
